context: finishing-led · walk-up, no lift or fire riser

brief.intro: Low-rise residential covers small walk-up apartment blocks or attached housing from ground plus one to ground plus three storeys — short enough that most building codes don't require a lift, a fire-fighting riser or complex vertical services. The structure is simple: a reinforced-concrete frame or load-bearing blockwork with flat RC slabs, built over two to four short storeys rather than a long repetitive tower cycle. Because there's little vertical MEP to coordinate, the whole programme is finishing-led — the pace is set by how fast the trade train (waterproofing, tiling, paint, fixtures) can move through each floor and unit, not by structural complexity or shaft coordination. This makes low-rise the simplest residential type to plan, but also the one where a stalled finishing trade has nowhere to hide — there's no long tower behind it to absorb the delay.

must_get_right: Close the roof (weather-tight) early — internal finishing below it cannot safely accelerate until the top is watertight.
Sequence blockwork so it doesn't box in first-fix services — chase and conduit routes must be agreed before walls go up.
Test wet-area waterproofing before tiling — the single biggest source of handover defects on this type.
Keep one continuous finishing trade train — with only 2–4 floors, any trade that falls behind has no floors of buffer to recover in.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Given the short duration of this project type, the network is kept simple — few summary bands, activities calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones, total float ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: A standard 6-day working calendar applies throughout. Finishing trades may add an extended day near handover to protect the completion date; there is little need for shift-based coordination given the building's short height.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs roof close-in (weather-tightness) → internal finishing trade train (plaster → screed/tiling → paint → fixtures) → snagging → handover. Because there are only two to four floors, the finishing train itself — not the structure — is almost always the critical path from an early date.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen before structure starts, since there are few floor repeats to amortise late changes across; a single mobilisation; one continuous finishing crew per trade covering the whole building rather than parallel crews per floor; no lift or fire-riser scope assumed.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Nothing on this project type is truly long-lead; the items below are tracked because they gate a specific trade front rather than because of extended lead times:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Small footprint sites typically have limited laydown and a single access point; one finishing crew often serves the whole building rather than parallel crews working floor by floor; boundary or party-wall constraints apply where the building is terraced or attached.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Roof waterproofing failure is the main technical risk; a weather delay to roof close-in cascades directly into finishing. Contingency is held after roof close-in and before handover, since there is little schedule depth elsewhere to absorb slippage.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (phase summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 lookahead for the field where useful — consistent with AACE 37R-06, kept simple given the short duration of this project type.
